_README.what: Curated seed list of consular-visa-delay mandamus/APA decisions, extracted from expert-authored practice advisories. This is SPEC.md section 14 tier 1 -- the free, highest-quality starting point, gathered before spending any API budget or money.
_README.why: The RECAP docket scraper can tell us WHAT happened to a case but rarely WHY, because docket-entry lines are terse and filed documents are PACER-gated. These advisories were written by practicing mandamus litigators who already read the opinions and grouped them by which government argument each one answers.
_README.important_caveat: Every 'advisory_characterization' below is the ADVISORY's summary of the holding, not an independent legal conclusion drawn by this project or by any AI. It is a pointer telling you which opinions are worth reading in full -- it is not a substitute for reading them. Verify before relying on any of it.
sources: NILA, 'Recent Trends in Immigration Delay Cases', 2026-05-17 (immigrationlitigation.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/2024.5.17-Recent-Trends-in-Immigration-Delay-Cases.pdf)
NILA / American Immigration Council, 'Mandamus and APA Delay Cases: Avoiding Dismissal and Proving the Case', 2021-02-19
_README.venue_note: User's case will be filed in the 9th Circuit (SPEC.md section 15). circuit=='9th' entries are the highest priority. D.D.C. entries are out-of-circuit but carry unusual weight -- most consular-delay litigation is filed there and its TRAC case law is the most developed.

direction_values.favorable_to_plaintiff: Advisory describes the court rejecting a government dismissal argument, or otherwise ruling in a way that helps a delay plaintiff.
direction_values.unfavorable_to_plaintiff: Advisory describes the court accepting a government argument / dismissing the delay claim.
direction_values.mixed: Court split the difference, or ruled favorably on one ground and adversely on another.

cases.advisory_characterization: Rejected the government's consular-nonreviewability argument; also placed among the courts holding TRAC review is not suitable at the motion-to-dismiss stage.
cases.priority_note: Top-tier: 9th Circuit AND squarely about administrative processing, the exact posture of a 221(g) delay.

cases.advisory_characterization: Listed among district courts that GRANTED the government's motion to dismiss after applying the TRAC factors.
cases.priority_note: Top-tier despite being adverse: 9th Circuit, same administrative-processing posture. Must be understood and distinguished.

cases.advisory_characterization: Held that TRAC-factor review is fact-intensive and not appropriate at the motion-to-dismiss stage before discovery.
cases.priority_note: 9th Circuit authority for defeating an early TRAC-based dismissal.

cases.advisory_characterization: Also held TRAC review inappropriate at the motion-to-dismiss stage pending factual development.
cases.priority_note: 9th Circuit; reinforces Akbar on the same procedural point.

cases.advisory_characterization: Found a nondiscretionary duty to adjudicate within a reasonable time under 5 U.S.C. 555(b), and held TRAC review inappropriate at the MTD stage.
cases.priority_note: 9th Circuit, favorable on BOTH the duty question and the TRAC-timing question.

cases.advisory_characterization: Found a nondiscretionary duty to schedule visa interviews within a reasonable time.
cases.priority_note: 9th Circuit; directly answers the government's 'no duty to act' argument.

cases.advisory_characterization: Dismissed the mandamus claim on the ground that the APA provides an adequate remedy at law.
cases.priority_note: 9th Circuit. Practical lesson: plead the APA claim, do not rely on the Mandamus Act alone.

cases.advisory_characterization: Granted the government's motion to dismiss after applying the TRAC factors.
cases.priority_note: 9th Circuit but different visa category; useful mainly to see what TRAC reasoning persuades a 9th Cir. district judge.

cases.advisory_characterization: Rejected the argument that a visa 'refusal' is a final decision triggering consular nonreviewability; agreed that while an application is still in administrative processing, even where a refusal has been relayed, the decision is not final, so unreasonable-delay claims are not barred.
cases.priority_note: Arguably THE central case for a 221(g) administrative-processing posture -- it defeats the government's most common threshold argument. Out-of-circuit but heavily cited.

cases.advisory_characterization: Rejected consular nonreviewability where no final decision has been rendered, so long as the plaintiff merely asks the court to require a decision regardless of its content. Also rejected the argument that plaintiffs lack standing against the Secretary of State as to the timing of adjudication, while dismissing claims against DHS/USCIS for lack of standing once the petition had moved to the NVC.
cases.priority_note: Extended analysis of nonreviewability (opinion pages 11-17). Also a caution on naming the right defendants.

cases.advisory_characterization: Rejected mootness for plaintiffs whose visas had been 'refused' after interview, finding such refusal often not final because a refusal may be entered for administrative processing. Also found a plausible claim of unreasonable delay under the TRAC factors.
cases.priority_note: Directly on point for 221(g): answers the 'your case is moot, it was already refused' argument.

cases.advisory_characterization: Among the courts rejecting the consular-nonreviewability bar in delay cases.
cases.priority_note: Recent D.D.C. reaffirmation.

cases.advisory_characterization: Found the claim against DHS and USCIS moot where USCIS had completed its processing before suit was filed.
cases.priority_note: Defendant-selection lesson: do not sue agencies that no longer hold the file.

cases.advisory_characterization: Granted the government's motion to dismiss after applying the TRAC factors.
cases.priority_note: Adverse D.D.C. TRAC analysis -- needs to be understood and distinguished.

cases.advisory_characterization: States that in the D.C. District Court the majority view is that it IS appropriate to apply the TRAC factors at the motion-to-dismiss stage.
cases.priority_note: Important contrast with the 9th Circuit cases above (Akbar, Salihi, Taherian, Iqbal), which hold the opposite. This split is a reason the 9th Circuit may be the better venue.

cases.case_name: Raouf v. U.S. Dep't of State
cases.advisory_characterization: Among the courts rejecting consular nonreviewability as a bar to delay claims.
cases.priority_note: Shows the nonreviewability holding is not confined to D.D.C.

cases.advisory_characterization: Found a nondiscretionary duty for embassies and the NVC to adjudicate visa petitions within a reasonable time; applied the Third Circuit's four-factor OCAWU test rather than TRAC and found analysis inappropriate at the MTD stage.
cases.priority_note: Useful for the duty argument; note the different circuit test.

cases.advisory_characterization: Found a nondiscretionary duty to review and adjudicate visa applications, that the pace is not committed to agency discretion by law, and a sufficient unreasonable-delay claim under TRAC -- noting discovery would matter especially for the first and fourth factors.
cases.priority_note: One of the more thoroughly favorable recent decisions.

cases.advisory_characterization: Rejected consular nonreviewability, but held that courts CAN consider the TRAC factors at the motion-to-dismiss stage.
cases.priority_note: Split result -- favorable on threshold, adverse on TRAC timing.

cases.case_name: Niknam v. U.S. Dep't of State
cases.advisory_characterization: Found that the Department of State does NOT have a nondiscretionary duty to schedule a visa interview for a family-based petition.
cases.priority_note: Direct counterpoint to Ghalambor (9th Cir.) on the identical question.

cases.advisory_characterization: Found no statutory or regulatory duty for the Department of State to review every visa petition.
cases.priority_note: Government relies on this line of authority.

cases.advisory_characterization: Found the nondiscretionary duty to adjudicate attaches only after the agency's investigation of the facts is complete.
cases.priority_note: This reasoning is dangerous in an administrative-processing case, since the government will argue the investigation is ongoing. Worth reading closely.

cases.advisory_characterization: Found jurisdiction over the claim to compel observance of the reasonable-time mandate, dismissed the separate mandamus claim as duplicative of the APA remedy, and granted dismissal on the TRAC factors.
cases.priority_note: Illustrates surviving the threshold arguments but still losing on TRAC.

cases.advisory_characterization: Found a nondiscretionary duty to review and adjudicate visa applications, but no duty to do so within a certain time frame absent claims of bad faith or abdication of responsibility.
cases.priority_note: Suggests pleading bad faith / abdication where the facts support it.

cases.advisory_characterization: Listed among recent D.D.C. consular-processing delay decisions.
cases.priority_note: Advisory lists it without characterizing the holding -- read to classify.

cases.advisory_characterization: Listed among recent D.D.C. consular-processing delay decisions.
cases.priority_note: Advisory lists it without characterizing the holding -- read to classify.

cases.advisory_characterization: Listed among recent D.D.C. consular-processing delay decisions.
cases.priority_note: Advisory lists it without characterizing the holding -- read to classify.

cases.advisory_characterization: Ordered the U.S. Consulate in Bombay to adjudicate immigrant visa applications, finding the consular officer had a duty to act (issue or refuse) under the regulations. Foundational 9th Circuit consular-mandamus precedent -- also cited elsewhere in the same advisory for dismissing claims against non-consulate defendants lacking power to issue visas.
cases.priority_note: One of the two 9th Circuit consular-nonreviewability precedents found in the 2021 advisory -- directly on point and binding-adjacent for the user's venue.

cases.advisory_characterization: Ordered the U.S. Consulate in Ciudad Juarez to adjudicate a regulatory request for reconsideration of a visa refusal.
cases.priority_note: Second 9th Circuit consular-nonreviewability precedent -- builds on Patel v. Reno within the same circuit.

cases.case_name: Nine Iraqi Allies Under Serious Threat Because of Their Faithful Serv. to the United States v. Kerry
cases.advisory_characterization: Held the doctrine of consular nonreviewability 'does not preclude Plaintiffs from challenging the Government's failure to decide.' Also found unreasonable delay where the statute provided a clear nine-month adjudication timeline (relevant to TRAC factors 1-2).
cases.priority_note: Frequently cited by later favorable D.D.C. decisions (Al-Gharawy, Giliana) as part of the same reasoning chain already in this seed list.

cases.advisory_characterization: Found jurisdiction over a mandamus claim seeking to compel the U.S. Embassy in Guyana to adjudicate an immigrant visa application.
cases.priority_note: Adds a 3rd Circuit data point showing the nonreviewability carve-out for delay claims is not confined to D.D.C. or the 9th Circuit.

foundational_authorities._what: Doctrine-defining cases every side cites -- these are not 'analogous outcomes' like the entries in 'cases', they ARE the legal standard. Direction doesn't cleanly apply; each has its own 'why_it_matters' instead.

entries.case_name: Telecommunications Research & Action Center v. FCC (TRAC)
entries.why_it_matters: The source of the six-factor 'TRAC factors' test that every single case in this seed list argues about. We had 27+ cases applying TRAC and never had TRAC itself. Essential background reading before drafting any TRAC-factor argument.

Supreme Court case the government's consular-nonreviewability argument typically rests on. Know what the other side will cite. Note: this was a due-process notice case about a visa denial, not a pure delay case -- later courts (Al-Gharawy, Giliana, Patel, Rivas, already in this seed) have distinguished delay claims from it.
The older Supreme Court foundation of consular nonreviewability, cited alongside Kerry v. Din. Same purpose: understand the doctrine's roots before arguing why it doesn't bar a delay claim.

D.C. Circuit case establishing the nonreviewability doctrine, but also cited approvingly (at 1159-60) by the favorable cases in this seed as consistent with allowing delay claims to proceed. Read both readings before relying on it either way.
